title: 02 — Iceberg Deletes, v3 and Maintenance
html:
02 — Iceberg Deletes, v3 and Maintenance

The one idea: data files are immutable, so a delete or an update is either a rewrite (copy-on-write) or a small note saying which rows no longer count (merge-on-read). Format v3 makes those notes much cheaper with deletion vectors, and adds row lineage, a variant type and more. Maintenance jobs keep the table fast and its storage bill sane.

1. What it is

This chapter covers four things:

  • Row-level changes: how DELETE, UPDATE and MERGE work when files can't be edited.
  • Format version 3: what the v3 spec adds, and who supports it as of October 2026.
  • Branches and tags: for write-audit-publish and releases.
  • Maintenance: expiring snapshots, compacting files, cleaning orphans. The v4 proposals are covered at the end.

2. Why it matters

  • Corrections and restatements are row-level changes. Their cost and their read penalty depend on the strategy you pick.
  • v3 features such as row lineage and variant change how you design tables, but you can't downgrade from v3 to v2, so every engine that reads the table must support v3 first.
  • Without maintenance, a busy table slows down (too many small files and delete files) and grows forever (expired data never freed).

3. The main ideas

3.1 Copy-on-write versus merge-on-read

Copy-on-write (CoW) Merge-on-read (MoR)
On delete or update Rewrite every affected data file without the old rows Write a small delete file (v2) or deletion vector (v3), plus new rows
Write cost High: rewrites whole files for one row Low
Read cost None extra Readers must apply deletes until compaction
Good for Rare, large changes. Read-heavy tables Frequent, small changes such as CDC and corrections
Set with write.delete.mode, write.update.mode, write.merge.mode table properties, each copy-on-write or merge-on-read

Delete files in v2:

  • Position deletes: "file X, row 42 is deleted".
  • Equality deletes: "every row where isin = 'INF…' is deleted". These are cheap to write, especially for streaming, but expensive to read.

Deletion vectors in v3: at most one deletion vector per data file, stored as a Roaring bitmap in a Puffin file. This replaces the pile of v2 position-delete files, so a reader merges one compact bitmap per file. Delta Lake uses the same approach.

3.2 What v3 adds

From the Iceberg spec, as checked 2026-10-26:

Feature What it gives you
Deletion vectors Cheap row-level deletes, at most one per data file
Row lineage Every row gets a stable _row_id and a _last_updated_sequence_number, so you can tell which rows changed in which commit. Existing rows get ids from the next rewrite on
Variant type Semi-structured (JSON-like) data stored efficiently, with optional shredding of common fields into real columns (see 04)
Default values Add a column with a default without rewriting files
New types Nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry and geography
Multi-argument transforms Partition or sort on transforms that take more than one column
Table encryption keys Spec support for encrypting table files

Who supports v3, as reported on 2026-10-26 (from vendor and secondary sources, so check before relying on it):

  • Snowflake reported v3 as GA in May 2026.
  • Databricks listed v3 as Public Preview from April 2026 (Runtime 18.0 and above).
  • AWS announced deletion vectors and row lineage in November 2025.
  • Trino's support was described as partial.
  • Iceberg Java 1.11.0 (released 2026-05-20) added deletion-vector and row-lineage support for v3.

3.3 Branches and tags

  • A branch is a named, movable line of snapshots. Use it for write-audit-publish: write to audit, check, then fast_forward main.
  • A tag is a named, fixed snapshot, for example a certified release 2026-10-23.v1. Created with ALTER TABLE ... CREATE TAG name [AS OF VERSION id] [RETAIN n DAYS]. Without RETAIN, it never expires.
  • Read either with VERSION AS OF 'name'.

3.4 Maintenance

Spark procedure (CALL catalog.system.<name>) What it does Why
expire_snapshots Drops old snapshots and the files only they referenced Frees storage, keeps metadata small. Tagged snapshots are kept
rewrite_data_files Compacts small files, applies deletes, can re-sort Read speed, fewer files to plan
rewrite_position_delete_files Compacts v2 position delete files Read speed on MoR tables
rewrite_manifests Regroups manifests to match query patterns Faster planning
remove_orphan_files Deletes files no snapshot references, such as leftovers from failed commits Storage cost

On Databricks, predictive optimization runs this kind of maintenance automatically for Unity Catalog managed tables (see 07).

3.5 Looking ahead: v4 proposals

As of August to October 2026, v4 is a set of proposals, not a released spec. They include:

  • an adaptive metadata tree, which enables single-file commits (a commit in the common case writes one object),
  • relative table paths, so tables can be moved,
  • column families,
  • an extensible statistics model.

There is also a reported proposal for Delta Lake to converge on the same metadata structure. Treat all of this as direction, not as something to build on.

4. Working code

The script deletes one row from a 100,000-row file both ways, then shows why many small deletes eventually call for compaction. Standard library only.

# Deleting one row from a 100,000-row data file, two ways.
ROWS = 100_000
data_file = [(i, f"INF{i:09d}", round(10 + i * 0.001, 3)) for i in range(ROWS)]
to_delete = {42_017}                                  # row position(s) to delete

# Copy-on-write (CoW): rewrite the whole file without the row. Expensive write, free read.
cow_new_file = [r for pos, r in enumerate(data_file) if pos not in to_delete]
print(f"CoW : rows written {len(cow_new_file):,}, read cost later: plain scan of 1 file")

# Merge-on-read (MoR) with a v3 deletion vector: write a tiny bitmap of deleted positions.
# Real Iceberg stores a Roaring bitmap in a Puffin file. Here a Python int is the bitmap.
dv = 0
for pos in to_delete:
    dv |= 1 << pos
dv_bytes = (dv.bit_length() + 7) // 8
print(f"MoR : rows written 0, deletion vector stored ({dv_bytes:,} bytes uncompressed here; "
      "a Roaring bitmap compresses a single set bit to a few bytes)")

def read_with_dv(file, dv):
    return [r for pos, r in enumerate(file) if not (dv >> pos) & 1]

live = read_with_dv(data_file, dv)
print(f"MoR read: {len(live):,} live rows, deleted row present: {any(r[0] == 42_017 for r in live)}")

# Many small deletes pile up; compaction (rewrite_data_files) folds them back into clean files.
for pos in range(0, ROWS, 10):                        # 10% of rows deleted over time
    dv |= 1 << pos
live = read_with_dv(data_file, dv)
print(f"After 10% deletes: readers filter {ROWS - len(live):,} rows on every scan -> time to compact")
compacted = live
print(f"Compaction: new file with {len(compacted):,} rows, deletion vector dropped")

Output:

CoW : rows written 99,999, read cost later: plain scan of 1 file
MoR : rows written 0, deletion vector stored (5,253 bytes uncompressed here; a Roaring bitmap compresses a single set bit to a few bytes)
MoR read: 99,999 live rows, deleted row present: False
After 10% deletes: readers filter 10,001 rows on every scan -> time to compact
Compaction: new file with 89,999 rows, deletion vector dropped

What to notice:

  • Copy-on-write wrote 99,999 rows to remove one. Merge-on-read wrote none.
  • The deletion vector here is a plain integer bitmap, about 5 KB because the set bit is far into it. A Roaring bitmap stores sparse positions in a few bytes, which is why v3 chose it.
  • After 10% deletes, every reader filters 10,001 rows on every scan. Compaction folds the deletes back into a clean file, and the read penalty disappears.

The Spark SQL equivalents, not run here (they need Spark with an Iceberg catalog named cat):

-- Not run.
ALTER TABLE cat.fin.nav SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'format-version' = '3',
  'write.delete.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.update.mode' = 'merge-on-read',
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'merge-on-read');

ALTER TABLE cat.fin.nav CREATE TAG `release_2026_10_23` RETAIN 3650 DAYS;

CALL cat.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'fin.nav');
CALL cat.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'fin.nav', older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-09-26 00:00:00', retain_last => 10);
CALL cat.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'fin.nav');

5. Common mistakes

  1. Upgrading to v3 before every reader supports it. You can't go back to v2.
  2. MoR without compaction. Reads get steadily slower as delete files pile up.
  3. Expiring snapshots you were relying on for audit. Tag what must be kept, and keep business history in columns.
  4. Running remove_orphan_files with a tiny age limit. It can delete files from a commit still in progress. Use a safe age (days, not minutes).
  5. Equality deletes everywhere. They are cheap to write but expensive to read. Prefer position deletes or deletion vectors where the engine supports them.

6. Exercise (1.5 hours)

  1. Extend the script: delete 1, 100 and 10,000 random rows, and record the CoW rows written against MoR bytes written. Draw the break-even point.
  2. Write a maintenance policy for a daily NAV table: when to compact, how many days of snapshots to keep, which releases to tag and for how long.
  3. If you have Spark with Iceberg, create a v2 table, set it to merge-on-read, run a DELETE, and look at the files and delete_files metadata tables.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. When is copy-on-write the better choice?
  2. What does a v3 deletion vector replace, and why is it cheaper to read?
  3. What does row lineage add to each row?
  4. Which maintenance procedure frees storage from old snapshots, and what protects a release from it?
  5. What is the status of Iceberg v4 as of October 2026?

Answers

  1. When changes are rare and large, and the table is read far more often than it is written.
  2. It replaces multiple v2 position delete files. There is at most one compact bitmap per data file, so readers merge one small structure.
  3. A stable _row_id and a _last_updated_sequence_number.
  4. expire_snapshots. Tags (and branches) keep their snapshots.
  5. Proposals with design documents and prototypes, not a released specification.

8. Sources
